evidence_quotes.quote: The implementation of the National Sanitation Campaign in Tanzania is analysed using the problem driven governance and political economy analysis methodology.
In total, 81 interviews or group discussions were carried out. Information was obtained from three regions, six districts, nine wards and 15 villages.
In the first year of the NSC, funds were not ready to use until 6 months after the start of the financial year, due to delays in transfers from central level.

evidence_quotes.criterion: effect_estimate and mechanism_flags (budget structure and per diems)
evidence_quotes.quote: Costs at district level mainly consist of district staff allowances for each community visit (45% on average) and fuel (20%).

Beyond general informative meetings, the flow of information between the Water, Education and Health departments was poor in general, as regards specific aspects where coordination could improve the impact of the programme.
only 20% of the villages visited had a clear and visible community action plan that could be consulted. In about 20% of places, triggering had been suspended because of low attendance.

country.comment: Empirical case study of the National Sanitation Campaign (NSC) in mainland rural Tanzania.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Abstract; PDF p. 4, Section 2.1; PDF p. 5, Section 2.2

effect_estimate.comment: Primary empirical findings are qualitative with descriptive process/implementation percentages from the first year of the NSC (2012-2013); Section 6 also cites contextual results from an unpublished impact evaluation of the predecessor TSSM pilot (~10% marginal increase in sanitation coverage and no detectable impact on open defecation in 10 districts), which is external context rather than this study's primary estimate.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported for household sanitation coverage impact. Direct implementation of Tanzania's National Sanitation Campaign (NSC) by District Health Departments fostered strong local government ownership and commitment, but service delivery effectiveness was constrained by rigid central planning rules, 6-month delays in central fund transfers, district allocations of 4.5–5 USD per targeted household (half the planned 10 USD/HH), staff per diems absorbing an average of 45% of district budgets (and fuel 20%) compared with 0–5% (2% average) for villager incentives, poor coordination among District Water, Education, and Health departments, weak downward accountability to villages, untrained and largely inactive village follow-up committees (only 20% of visited villages had a visible community action plan and CLTS triggering was suspended in about 20% of places due to low attendance), a 40% error rate in checked baseline questionnaires, and weak mason training and supply chains (sanplat slabs priced at 3–5 USD, rising to 8 USD in the highest-demand village, with upfront material payment barriers and no community solidarity safety nets for vulnerable households).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 8, Section 3.3; PDF pp. 10–12, Sections 4.1–4.3; PDF pp. 13–14, Sections 5–6

mechanism_certainty.comment: Primary qualitative case study (appraised with CASP; design ceiling = 2) that directly observes and documents decentralized planning, intergovernmental fiscal transfer delays, per diem rules, inter-departmental fragmentation, community participation burdens, and mason support rules operating during NSC implementation across 6 districts and 15 villages.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 5, Section 2.2; PDF pp. 7–12, Sections 3.2–4.4

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines centralized online project planning and community targeting (planning), 6-month central transfer delays (delay), absence of subsidies or safety nets for vulnerable elders/disabled households under the household self-financing policy (hardship_exception), CLTS community triggering and unpaid villager monitoring/data collection versus staff per diems (participation), fragmentation across four ministries and district Water/Education/Health departments (institutional_fragmentation), intergovernmental fiscal/political relations between central ministries, district technicians, and elected ward/village leaders (political_coordination), and district facilitation, mason training, and slab mould lending (bureaucratic_assistance).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, planning, delay, hardship_exception, participation, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination, bureaucratic_assistance
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 6–8, Sections 3.1–3.3; PDF pp. 9–12, Sections 4.1–4.4, Table 2; PDF pp. 12–13, Section 5

outcome_flags.comment: Focuses on rural household access to improved sanitation / elimination of open defecation (ODF status), household sanitation coverage targets under the NSC, and affordability of latrine slabs and upfront material costs for rural and vulnerable households.
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 2–4, Sections 1.1–1.2; PDF p. 6, Section 3.1; PDF p. 8, Section 3.3; PDF pp. 9–12, Sections 4.1 & 4.3

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Primary qualitative case study using Problem-Driven Governance and Political Economy Analysis based on document review, semi-structured interviews, and group discussions (non-representative questionnaire spot-checks are ancillary to qualitative process assessment).
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF pp. 4–6, Sections 2.1–2.2; PDF p. 11, Section 4.3

sample_size.comment: Purposive sample of 6 districts out of 42 districts implementing the NSC in 2012–2013; all except one invited participant agreed to participate.
sample_size.value: 81 interviews or group discussions across 3 regions, 6 districts, 9 wards, and 15 villages (12 national-level, 8 regional-level, 26 district-level, and 35 ward- and village-level interviews)

study_design.comment: Qualitative governance and political economy case study conducted during the first financial year of NSC implementation (mid-2012 to mid-2013).
study_design.value: Qualitative case study using Problem-Driven Governance and Political Economy Analysis (PGPE), combining policy/document review with semi-structured interviews and group discussions across purposively sampled districts, wards, and villages
